# Volume 3 — Chapter XXXV The Last Wexcombe Year Opens

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

Taking a seat upon a travel bag while exhaling with delight, Cressy remarked, “We have all returned to this spot, pleasantly tanned and delighting like a powerful athlete entering a contest.” She continued, “Is it not wonderful to behold this beloved former Tabby’s Place once more—along with Aunty—and the felines? Has Smudge not suffered the loss of yet one more portion of his ear?”
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0000 }

“If he were completely without ears, Smudge would be the sweetest cat anywhere,” stated Nell faithfully from her trunk, as Smudge twisted around her lap in a wild burst of greeting.
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0001 }

“Aren’t you happy to see that we have returned, Aunty?” asked Cressy.
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0002 }

“Yes. However, I want you to put things in order,” Aunt Euphemia said mournfully, regarding the dense tangle of trunks and suitcases that enveloped the four laughing, babbling girls. “You are able to speak equally well at a later time. My rule when I was a girl was work before play.”
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0003 }

“Oh, we’ve only inverted that in our generation, Aunty. Our principle is to enjoy your fun before applying yourself. Your tasks can be done far more effectively once you’ve enjoyed a proper stretch of recreation.”
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0004 }

“If a minister is to be your husband,” Aunt Euphemia remarked, gathering Joseph alongside her knitting work and surrendering to what was bound to happen with the captivating elegance that rendered her the finest of housemothers, “words like ‘dig in’ must be abandoned by you.”
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0005 }

“Why?” Cressy groaned. “Oh, why is a minister’s wife expected to speak nothing but prunes and prisms? I will not. Everyone on Tanner Street uses slang—which means, metaphorical language—and if I failed to do so, they would consider me unbearably arrogant and stuck up.”
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0006 }

“Have you broken the news to your family?” Honora asked, offering pieces from her lunchbasket to the Sarah-cat.
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0007 }

Cressy gave a nod.
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0008 }

“In what manner did they react to it?”
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0009 }

“Oh, mother flew into a rage. However, I remained steadfast—even I, Cressida Lindsay, who had never previously been able to stand firm on anything. Father proved more composed. Father’s very own father served as a minister, which explains why he possesses a warm feeling toward the clergy. Following mother’s cooling down, I brought Ez to Mount Holly, and both of them adored him. Nevertheless, mother dropped several terrifying insinuations during each chat about the expectations she had held for me. Oh, my holiday trail has not precisely been sprinkled with roses, dear girls. Still—I have triumphed and I possess Ez. No other thing counts.”
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0010 }

“For your part,” Aunt Euphemia uttered grimly.
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0011 }

“And not to Ez, either,” Cressy fired back. “You continue to feel sorry for him. For what reason, if I may ask? I believe he is worthy of envy. In me, he is gaining intellect, loveliness, and a heart made of gold.”
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0012 }

“We are fortunate to understand how your remarks should be received,” Aunt Euphemia remarked with patience. “I trust that you refrain from speaking in such a manner in the presence of strangers. What impression would be made upon them?”
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0013 }

“Oh, discovering their thoughts is not something I desire. Seeing my own reflection through the eyes of other people holds no appeal for me. It would, I am certain, prove terribly unpleasant on most occasions. Furthermore, Burns’s sincerity regarding that plea seems doubtful to me.”
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0014 }

“Ah, it seems to me that everyone asks in prayer for certain outcomes that are actually undesired, provided we possess sufficient honesty to examine our inner selves,” Aunt Euphemia admitted frankly. “My belief is that those kinds of petitions fail to ascend very high. In times past, I offered prayers for the ability to pardon a particular individual, yet I am currently aware that pardoning her was not my genuine wish. Once I at last reached the point of truly desiring to do so, my forgiveness was granted to her devoid of any need for prayer.”
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0015 }

“It is hard for me to imagine you holding a grudge for very long,” Mabel remarked.
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0016 }

“Oh, I was in the past. However, bearing a grudge appears to be a waste of time as one grows older.”
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0017 }

“That brings it to mind,” remarked Nell, and related the story of John and Thora.
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0018 }

“And now give us the details of that romantic encounter you alluded to so mysteriously in a letter of yours,” Cressy requested.
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0019 }

With vivid energy, Nell performed Samuel’s marriage offer. The girls uttered shrill cries of mirth, and Aunt Euphemia let out a smile.
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0020 }

“Deriding your suitors lacks propriety,” she declared sternly; “however,” she continued composedly, “it was my own constant habit.”
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0021 }

“Aunty, do tell us about your beaux,” Cressy begged, adding, “There must have been so many of them.”
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0022 }

“They aren’t in the past tense,” Aunt Euphemia countered. “I still have them. Back home, three elderly widowers have been eyeing me affectionately for a while now. You young people shouldn’t assume that all the world's romance belongs to you.”
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0023 }

“ Aunty, widowerhood and making eyes at someone hardly seem romantic.”
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0024 }

“Well, no; yet young people are not always full of romance either. A few of my suitors definitely were not. I would laugh at them outrageously, poor young men. Saul Elwood was one—he existed in a kind of waking trance constantly—never appeared to grasp what was happening around him. He failed to realize that I had answered ‘no’ until a year had passed after I said it. Once he actually got married, his spouse tumbled out of the sleigh a certain night while they were traveling back from church, and he failed to notice she was gone. Next came Dan Winston. He possessed too much knowledge. He was aware of everything in this world along with the majority of what exists in the hereafter. He had the ability to provide an answer to any query, even had you inquired of him the date of the Judgment Day. Milton Edwards was truly pleasant and I was fond of him, yet I did not become his wife. On the one hand, he required a week to comprehend a joke, and on the other hand he failed to ever propose to me. Horatio Reeve proved to be the most captivating suitor I ever possessed. However, whenever he related a tale he embellished it so thoroughly that you were unable to discern it beneath the adornments. I was never capable of determining if he was fabricating or merely allowing his fantasy to wander free.”
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0025 }

“And as for the rest of them, Aunty?”
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0026 }

“Depart and open your bags,” Aunt Euphemia uttered, accidentally brandishing Joseph in their direction instead of a needle. “The rest possessed too much kindness to mock. I will hold their memory in honor. A box containing blossoms is located in your room, Nell. Their arrival occurred approximately sixty minutes back.”
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0027 }

Once the initial week had passed, the students residing at Tabby’s Place established a routine of rigorous academic work; indeed, this marked their final year at Wexcombe, requiring continuous effort to secure commencement accolades. Nell applied herself to English studies, Honora immersed herself in the classics, and Cressida labored intensively at Mathematics. At times weariness overtook them, at times despair set in, and at times no goal appeared deserving of their exertions. It was during a period of such despondency that Mabel made her way up to the blue room on a wet night in November. Nell was seated on the floor within a small ring of illumination produced by the lamp situated next to her, encircled by a multitude of discarded, balled-up papers.
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0028 }

“Whatever are you up to?”
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0029 }

“I was merely examining a few old Story Club tales. My goal was to find a bit of cheer and inebriation. Having studied to the point where everything appeared azure, I headed up here to retrieve these from my trunk. Because they are so thoroughly soaked in tragedy and tears, they prove to be excruciatingly funny.”
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0030 }

“I’m feeling down and disheartened too,” Mabel stated, flinging herself onto the sofa. “Nothing appears to have any value. Even my thoughts are ancient. I’ve already pondered every single one. What purpose does life serve anyway, Nell?”
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0031 }

“Darling, our feeling like this is simply caused by brain fatigue, as well as the weather. Following a tough day of work, a night with heavy rain such as this one would crush the spirits of anybody except a Mark Tapley. You are aware that life is worth living.”
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0032 }

“Ah, I guess that is the case. Still, I am unable to demonstrate it to my own satisfaction at this moment.”
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0033 }

“Only consider every one of the grand and virtuous spirits that have existed and labored throughout the earth,” Nell remarked in a dreamy manner. “Is it not valuable to follow in their footsteps and receive the legacy of their achievements and lessons? Is it not valuable to believe that we are able to partake in their encouragement? Furthermore, what about every grand spirit destined to arrive in times to come? Is it not valuable to labor a bit and pave the road for those individuals—rendering merely a single stride along their course simpler?”
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0034 }

“Oh, Nell, my intellect concurs with what you say. Nevertheless, my spirit continues to be gloomy and lacking in creative spark. Rainy evenings perpetually leave me feeling filthy and unkempt.”
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0035 }

“On certain nights the rain appeals to me—lying in bed, I enjoy listening to it tap against the roof and sweep among the pine trees.”
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0036 }

“I am fond of it when it remains upon the roof,” Mabel stated. “That is not invariably the case. During the previous summer, I passed a dreadful night inside an ancient country farmhouse. Rain trickled through the leaking roof and tapped against my bed. That held no romance at all. In the ‘mirk midnight’ I was forced to rise and bustle about to drag the bedstead away from the leak—and it happened to be a heavy, old-fashioned bed that weighed roughly a ton. Following that, the continuous drip-drop, drip-drop persisted through the whole night until my nerves were completely shattered. You cannot imagine how spine-chilling a sound a large raindrop produces when it hits an uncovered floor with a mushy thud during the night. It resembles spectral footsteps and similar horrors. Why are you laughing, Nell?”
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0037 }

“Such tales. As Cressy might remark, they are dyingly funny—in multiple ways, because every character perished within them. What exceptionally beautiful heroines were ours—and in what fashion we attired them!
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0038 }

“Silks, satins, velvets, jewels, and laces were the only things they ever put on. In one of Odette Pullen’s tales, a narrative portrays the protagonist as slumbering in a gorgeous nightshirt made of white satin and adorned with seed pearls.”
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0039 }

“Continue,” Mabel urged. “It seems to me that existence remains valuable so long as it contains something to laugh at.”
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0040 }

“I wrote this particular one. My female protagonist is enjoying herself at a dance, ‘glittering from head to foot with large diamonds of the first water.’ Yet of what use were beauty or expensive clothing? ‘The paths of glory lead but to the grave.’ It was unavoidable that they be killed or perish from a broken heart. For them, no way out existed.”
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0041 }

“Allow me to look through a few of your tales.”
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0042 }

“Well, here is my masterpiece. Take note of its happy title—‘My Graves.’ Quarts of tears were shed by me when I wrote it, and gallons were shed by the other girls when it was read by me. Odette Pullen’ mother gave her a frightful scolding due to the fact that she possessed so many handkerchiefs in the wash during that week. A harrowing tale, it concerns the wanderings of the wife of a Methodist minister. The reason I made her a Methodist was that it was required for her to wander. In every place she resided, she buried a child. Nine of them existed, and their graves, severed far apart, ranged from Newfoundland to Vancouver. The children were described by me, their several death beds were pictured, and their tombstones and epitaphs were detailed. The burial of the entire nine had been intended by me, but after eight had been disposed of by me, my invention of horrors ran out, and the ninth was permitted by me to live as a hopeless cripple.”
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0043 }

As Mabel perused My Graves, breaking up its mournful passages with quiet laughs, and Smudge enjoyed the righteous slumber of a feline that had spent the whole night curled atop an Odette Pullen story about a lovely fifteen-year-old girl who left to care for lepers—naturally succumbing to the terrible illness in the end—Nell skimmed the remaining manuscripts and remembered the past at Brierley school, where the members of the Story Club used to compose them while seated beneath the spruce trees or nestled amid the brookside ferns. What an enjoyable time they had shared! The warmth and joy of those former summer days flooded back to her as she read. Neither all the splendour of Greece nor all the majesty of Rome possessed the power to cast a spell like those amusing, sorrowful stories from the Story Club. Within the collection of manuscripts, Nell discovered one recorded on pieces of packing paper. Amused laughter flooded her gray eyes when she remembered when and where it was created. It was the piece she had composed on the day she dropped through the roof of the Cobb duckhouse along the Tory Road.
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0044 }

Nell cast a quick look at it, and then she began reading it with deep concentration. The piece was a short conversation among asters, sweet-peas, wild canaries occupying the lilac bush, and the protective spirit of the garden. Having finished reading it, she remained seated, gazing blankly ahead; then, once Mabel had departed, she pressed flat the wrinkled manuscript.
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0045 }

“I think I shall,” she stated with determination.
{: #nw-v03-c35-p0046 }
